The answer is not to abolish the privacy. It is to bound what any vote can decide, so that capturing one voting mechanism cannot confer control over the whole system. Part 1 : An Ode to Rough Consensus . Part 2 : When We Disagree: Making Rough Consensus Work . Part 3 : Governance in a Shielded World. Zcash is building a parallel financial system, outside of but adjacent to the existing one. Its governance, however, remains entirely inside human institutions. That private financial system starts from a different assumption from the one we have become accustomed to elsewhere: privacy is normal. In such a system, private by default should be the ordinary situation, not a special mode for people with something to hide. Traditional finance already runs part of its markets this way. Dark pools let large investors trade without displaying their orders, so that others cannot trade against them. Dark does not mean lawless. events.excerpt: Hi everyone. I’m Leandro, a full-stack developer and open-source contributor with experience in AI, blockchain, web and mobile development, and developer tooling. I recently submitted a grant proposal for Zcash Wallet Devtools , an open-source toolkit designed to improve the developer experience when building applications with Zcash. What’s the idea? Integrating Zcash wallets and payment requests into web applications can be challenging to debug. Developers often need to rely on console logs, manually inspect SDK responses, and troubleshoot different wallet behaviors. I’d like to make that process easier by building a lightweight, privacy-aware debugging toolkit inspired by tools like React Query Devtools and Solana’s Connector Debugger. What will it include? TypeScript SDK: Instrumentation for wallet connections, events, state changes, and errors. Interactive Devtools Dashboard: A visual panel that runs inside applications during development. ZIP-321 Diagnostics: Inspect payment request lifecycle events and troubleshoot integration issues. Privacy-Aware Logging: Protect sensitive wallet information by default. Wallet Integration: Initial support for one compatible Zcash wallet SDK. Next.js Demo: A working example showing how everything integrates. Bilingual Documentation: Technical guides and examples in English and Spanish. Open Source: MIT license, automated tests, and npm publication. Grant details Requested funding: $3,000 USD This includes $500 in startup funding and $2,500 distributed across four development milestones. Estimated development time: Approximately 8 wee

events.excerpt: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post . The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when

events.excerpt: We propose an institution-managed user payment ledger for recording account debits and credits, enforcing spending capacity, and sealing account periods independently of funds settlement. Specification Draft PR #2159 Problem and scope A payment institution needs to distinguish a customer’s business entries from changes to the spending capacity it grants. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. This proposal defines a common contract interface for those records and controls. It can serve an institution’s own business independently or compose with an on-chain payment protocol. It does not issue or transfer assets, establish customer identity, or prove that funds have been frozen or settled. Account model and interface Each account is scoped by (account, institution) . An institution can serve payer accounts, merchant accounts, or both; the same address at two institutions does not share records or capacity. Holding the account’s private key does not grant permission to write entries. Current state contains a limit baseline, cumulative outflows and inflows, and a user-period identifier: available = limit + credit - debit The three amounts and the resulting available capacity must fit in uint96 ; arithmetic uses wider intermediates and rejects negative capacity or out-of-range results. Five write operations separate the relevant responsibilities: addLimit and subLimit adjust the baseline without changing business-entry totals
